source.title: Scaling Laws in Linear Regression: Compute, Parameters, and Data
source.authors: Li-Cong Lin; Jingfeng Wu; S. Kakade; Peter L. Bartlett; Jason D. Lee

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and appendix are present.
record.tranche_reason: It analyzes and simulates scaling of population squared error in sketched linear regression, rather than measuring language-model cross-entropy. This is a conceptual test of power-law scaling and compute allocation using a different model and measure.
record.gate_note: Rows record the paper’s own theoretical bounds, compute-allocation results, and simulations. The cited language-model scaling results and the cited finding about multiple data passes are not results from this study and are not rows. The paper does not test predictions from small runs against much larger runs.
record.test_reason: The study proves risk bounds and runs synthetic simulations for sketched linear regression trained by one-pass or averaged SGD, measured by population squared error. It trains no language model and measures no held-out pretraining loss, so its results do not bear on V1–V7 as stated. It explains scaling-law form with a linear analogue rather than testing the claim. The reader's 'tests/T2' and its V1/V3/V7 labels are therefore not adopted, and the findings go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors prove matching bounds Θ(M^-(a−1) + N^-(a−1)/a) for sketched linear regression with one-pass SGD, with variance of higher order due to SGD's implicit regularization. They conjecture that clean empirical LM scaling laws reflect this vanishing variance in underfitted, single- or few-pass training. They cite multi-epoch departures (Muennighoff et al.) as consistent with this view but do not test it.
record.recipe_differences: Unlike the original language-model studies, this paper uses Gaussian-sketch linear regression, one-pass or averaged SGD, population squared error, theoretical bounds, and synthetic simulations. It does not measure transformer pretraining cross-entropy or test empirical small-to-large-run extrapolation.
record.method_sensitivity: The results vary with covariance spectral form and degree, source-condition exponent b, and training procedure: geometrically decayed last-iterate SGD uses Neff = N/log(N), while fixed-step averaged SGD uses N. The compute-optimal allocation also depends on a or b.

fits_no_version.finding: In sketched linear regression with power-law covariance spectrum (degree a) and one-pass SGD, reducible risk is Θ(M^-(a−1)) + Θ(Neff^-(a−1)/a). Variance is higher-order and so vanishes from the fit. Simulations recover the exponents, e.g. fitted (0.54, 0.34) vs predicted (0.5, 0.33).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Additive power-law risk in model and data size arises provably in linear models trained with strongly regularizing (one-pass) SGD.

fits_no_version.finding: In the linear model with C=MN, the optimal split is M ~ C^(1/(a+1)) and N ~ C^(a/(a+1)), or with b in place of a under a source condition. The split thus depends on spectrum and task exponents.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In solvable linear models, compute-optimal allocation exponents are set by the data spectrum and target decay.

fits_no_version.finding: Under a source condition the exponents become b−1 and (b−1)/a; under a log-power-law spectrum the risk is polylogarithmic in M and N rather than a power law.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In linear models, the scaling-law exponents and even the power-law form depend on spectrum and prior assumptions.

record.problems: The results concern linear regression rather than language models and rely on stated Gaussian-design, prior, spectrum, and SGD assumptions. Simulations use finite-dimensional synthetic data; the paper does not test small-run extrapolation to larger language-model runs. Several simulation values are reported in figure captions rather than tables.

untested.parts: No language-model pretraining loss is measured; only linear-regression population risk.
No LM compute-optimal allocation is tested; the allocation derived is for a linear proxy with C=MN.
No other modality or neural training regime is tested; the paper only cites Muennighoff et al. on repeated data.
No comparison of fitting choices or published LM laws.

missing.what: For b ≥ a+1, the upper and lower bounds do not match (a gap left open). This is a regime where the paper's theory does not determine the scaling form.

record.verdict_notes: This is a theoretical, toy-model study. A researcher who counts linear-model analogues as an 'other training regime' might link the fits_no_version findings to V5 as supportive. That is not done here, because V5's examples are neural models in other modalities and regimes. The reader's V3 'challenges' label was in any case unsupported: a linear proxy allocation cannot contradict LM allocations.

versions.untested_parts: Tests population squared error in sketched linear regression under specified spectral and prior assumptions, not held-out pretraining loss in language models or actual language-model scaling over several orders of magnitude.
Does not fit laws on small runs and evaluate their predictions on runs orders of magnitude larger.
Derives an optimal allocation under its linear-regression compute definition; does not establish the language-model allocation trend or test Kaplan’s and Hoffmann’s empirical allocations directly.
Does not vary depth, width, or neural-network architecture.
Does not test other modalities, repeated-data language-model training, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Does not evaluate downstream task performance.

Shows dependence on spectral and prior assumptions and training procedure in its theoretical setting; does not compare parameter-counting conventions, fitting methods, or language-model datasets, and does not empirically demonstrate curves bending in language-model runs.

rows.subject: sketched linear regression
rows.size_stated: M trainable parameters; N sketched data
rows.stage_stated: one-pass SGD with geometrically decaying stepsizes
rows.operation_detail: Theorem 4.1 derives population-risk scaling under a power-law covariance spectrum and isotropic parameter prior.
rows.value: σ² + Θ(1/M^(a−1)) + Θ(1/(Neff γ)^((a−1)/a)); the text also states the reducible risk is Θ(M^(−(a−1)) + N^(−(a−1)/a)) in the abstract.
rows.uncertainty: Bounds hold with probability at least 1 − e^(−Ω(M)) over S; hidden constants depend on a.
rows.note: The result is for expected population squared error in the stated linear-regression setup, not language-model cross-entropy. The theorem also states that variance is higher order than approximation and bias in this regime.
rows.check: Theorem 4.1 bound for sketched linear regression, not language-model pretraining loss; also mixes the theorem's Neff·γ form with the abstract's N form.

rows.subject: sketched linear regression
rows.operation_detail: Derives the allocation minimizing population risk for compute C = MN.
rows.measure: Risk-minimizing model size and data size under fixed compute
rows.uncertainty: The Θ̃ notation hides logarithmic factors.
rows.locator: Section 4, “Allocation of data and model sizes,” p. 6; Theorem 6.1 referenced
rows.note: The text says this allocation assigns data size slightly larger than model size when compute is the bottleneck.
rows.check: Derived allocation (M ~ C^(1/(a+1)), N ~ C^(a/(a+1))) for a linear-regression compute proxy C=MN. It cannot confirm or contradict LM compute-optimal allocation, so the reader's V3 'challenges' label is unfounded.

rows.subject: sketched linear regression
rows.size_stated: M trainable parameters; N sketched data
rows.stage_stated: one-pass SGD with geometrically decaying stepsizes
rows.operation_detail: Theorem 4.2 derives risk scaling under an anisotropic source condition.
rows.value: σ² + Θ(1/M^(b−1)) + Θ(1/(Neff γ)^((b−1)/a)) + Θ(min{M,(Neff γ)^(1/a)}/Neff)
rows.uncertainty: Bounds hold with probability at least 1 − e^(−Ω(M)) over S; constants may depend on (a,b).
rows.note: The paper says the variance term is dominated by approximation and bias when 1 < b ≤ a; for a < b < a + 1, it remains dominated if the stepsize is optimally tuned.
rows.check: Theorem 4.2 under source condition; a theoretical linear-model result, not fit dependence in published LM laws.

rows.measure: Risk-minimizing model size, data size, and stepsize under fixed compute
rows.uncertainty: The Θ̃ notation hides logarithmic factors.
rows.note: This allocation depends on source-condition exponent b as well as compute.
rows.check: Allocation under source condition in the linear model; not an LM allocation.

rows.check: Log-power-law spectrum yields polylog risk in the linear model; this is not an observation of LM curves bending.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Power-law spectrum, stated prior and SGD settings in the linear-regression theory and simulations
reader_labels.reason: The derived risk bounds and reported fitted exponents show power-law risk scaling in parameter and data sizes in this setting (r1–r7, r12–r18).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Fixed compute C = MN in the stated linear-regression setup
reader_labels.reason: The paper derives stable compute powers for both model size and data size (r8, r10).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Relative model/data growth in the paper’s fixed-compute allocation
reader_labels.reason: For the isotropic case, the derived data-size exponent a/(a+1) exceeds the model-size exponent 1/(a+1), rather than model size growing faster than data or both growing equally (r8).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Changes to spectral degree, source condition, and SGD averaging procedure in the theoretical setting
reader_labels.reason: The derived risk exponents and optimal allocations depend on spectrum/source assumptions, and the averaged-iterate result uses N rather than Neff in its data term (r1, r8–r12).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The derived risk depends on powers of logarithms under this spectrum, rather than the power-law-spectrum risk formula (r11).
